clue.text: A boy in sporting association with a Mohammedan girl

indicators.note: the boy's name is set inside the letters for the sporting body plus the clue's opening A

parts.note: FA is the Football Association, English football's governing body
Tim is a boy's name

explanation.surface: Some lad is seen in a sporting club alongside a Muslim girl.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's opening 'A' is not a link word: it supplies the last letter, with TIM sitting between FA and A.
explanation.definitionFit: Fatima was the Prophet Muhammad's daughter, and her name remains a common one for Muslim girls.

parts.note: painters of an early twentieth-century movement named after what is still to come, read as artists whose time is not yet here

explanation.surface: A dismissive remark about painters still awaiting success.
explanation.definitionFit: The members of the Italian avant-garde movement led by Marinetti took their name from the time still to come.

indicators.note: the letter for love is placed inside the word litter before the shuffle
something unusual is out of its normal order, so the letters of the whole phrase are rearranged

parts.note: love is nil in tennis scoring, which looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A quoted phrase about affection among a brood is called a strange piece of verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts O inside LITTER, giving LITTOER, and 'unusual' rearranges those seven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A triolet is a short eight-line verse form with repeated lines, so it is a kind of poem.

clue.text: He hates the girls for hiding the missing toy

indicators.note: a hiding is a thrashing, and a thrashed set of letters is knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: A misanthropic man conceals a lost plaything from some girls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hiding' looks like concealment but is a beating, the anagram signal for MISSING TOY; 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A misogynist is a man who dislikes or distrusts women.

definitions.meaning: wayward means contrary or wilfully stubborn
a poet might be paid at a rate for each verse, split into two Latin-style words

explanation.surface: A rebellious poet asks whether this is how he gets his fee.
explanation.definitionFit: Perverse behaviour is contrary and obstinate, the same as wayward conduct; the second reading splits it as 'per verse'.

clue.text: Establishes three points about a drinking fine

indicators.note: the three compass letters go round the other piece, surrounding it

parts.note: E, N and S are three compass points: east, north, south
a sconce was an Oxford college forfeit, a tankard of ale the offender had to drain

explanation.surface: Someone sets up a rule that three items cover a penalty for drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: A SCONCE was an old Oxford college penalty for breaking table etiquette at dinner: the offender had to down a large tankard of ale.
explanation.definitionFit: To ensconce is to settle or install someone firmly, the same as establishing them.

definitions.meaning: a bench tool that holds work in a firm grip

explanation.surface: A fortress of wickedness, such as a den of iniquity.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the clamping tool on a workbench that grips strongly; the other is moral wickedness.

clue.text: With unearned income he has the right to go in about one

indicators.note: the verb for going in wraps round the numeral, enclosing it

parts.note: to go in is to enter
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A man of private means is entitled to enter, round about one o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' is a link word; the definition is a full description of the person.
explanation.definitionFit: A rentier is a person living on investment or property income rather than wages.

parts.note: describes happening afterwards, following on from something earlier

explanation.surface: An instruction introducing a list of what will happen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as follows' looks like a phrase introducing a list; here it means 'in sequence', describing a later happening.
explanation.definitionFit: To ensue is to happen afterwards or as a result, so it means to occur in sequence.

indicators.note: back means the word is read from right to left

parts.note: tots are small children

explanation.surface: Guide the youngsters home again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steer' looks like a verb, but it is the noun for a young castrated bullock; STOT is a Scots and northern English word for one.
explanation.definitionFit: A stot is a young bullock, a castrated male calf raised for beef, which is what a steer is.

parts.note: reads like a tennis pairing but describes a woman's matching cardigan and jumper sold together as a pair

explanation.surface: A tennis doubles pair of women who are evenly matched.
explanation.walkthrough: The print has 'Ladies'' with an apostrophe; tennis's Ladies' Doubles misleads.
explanation.definitionFit: A twinset is a woman's matching jumper and cardigan worn together, so it is a well-matched double garment.

definitions.meaning: to second a motion or a person is to back them

explanation.surface: Someone backs something for a little while.
explanation.definitionFit: Seconding a proposal backs it in a debate, and seconds are also the sixtieth parts of a minute.

clue.text: In relation, for example, to being sent down

indicators.note: the abbreviation sits inside the word relation, as the clue literally says

parts.note: EG is the abbreviation for exempli gratia, for example

explanation.surface: A remark about being expelled, in relation to an example.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening 'In relation' reads as a stock phrase but literally places EG in RELATION; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Relegation is demotion to a lower division or rank, as when a football team drops down.

definitions.meaning: a pit is a coal working dug into the ground
an owner claims a thing by saying it belongs to him

explanation.surface: A colliery owner declares his right to the coal.
explanation.definitionFit: A mine is a colliery or excavation, and 'mine!' is what a possessor says to claim something.

definitions.meaning: enduring means suffering or experiencing something
going on the London Underground, the Tube, is going below ground

explanation.surface: Putting up with a journey on the London Underground.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tube is London's underground railway, so travelling by it is 'under going'.
explanation.definitionFit: Undergoing something means experiencing or suffering it; the cryptic reading splits it into below plus travelling.

clue.text: Do these mills on the other hand grind fast ?

definitions.text: Do these mills on the other hand grind fast ?

parts.words: Do these mills on the other hand grind fast
parts.note: the mills of God grind slowly, so the Devil's mills, the opposite, must grind quickly

explanation.surface: A question about whether certain factories work at speed.
explanation.walkthrough: Two allusions meet: the proverb that 'the mills of God grind slowly', and Blake's 'dark Satanic mills' in the hymn Jerusalem; the Devil's mills are the opposite of God's.
explanation.definitionFit: Devilish, belonging to the Devil, who is the opposite of God; Blake called the factories of industrial England 'dark Satanic mills'.

parts.note: the pull of liquid up a hair-thin tube, the physics effect named from Latin for hair

explanation.surface: What makes someone's locks appealing.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests beautiful hair; the clue means the physical effect that draws water up narrow tubes, named from Latin capillus, hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Capillary means hair-like, from Latin for hair, and capillary attraction draws liquid up a very fine tube.

clue.text: Kicked in red cent in part exchange

indicators.note: goods traded in part exchange change hands, so these letters are swapped round into new places

explanation.surface: A coin was handed over in a trade-in deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kicked in' looks like 'chipped in' money; it is football: crossing the ball into the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: In football, to centre is to kick the ball from the wing into the middle of the pitch, so centred is kicked it in.

indicators.note: how asks in what manner, so the name and verb are taken in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Asking about the death of a man named Clyde, firmly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'How' asks the manner, and the letters of CLYDE DIED rearranged give the adverb answering it.
explanation.definitionFit: Decidedly means unquestionably or without doubt.

clue.text: Makes a mockery of dispatches to higher levels

definitions.meaning: to parody or ridicule someone by imitation
sends someone upward, as to a higher floor or rank

explanation.surface: Someone ridicules messages sent to senior staff.
explanation.definitionFit: To parody is a sense of the phrasal verb, while its literal sense is to post something upward.

clue.text: William & Co. provide the standard short answer

parts.note: a norm is a standard or usual level
ANS is the abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: William's firm supplies the usual brief reply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'William & Co.' looks like a firm's name; it is William the Conqueror and his followers.
explanation.definitionFit: William the Conqueror led the invaders who conquered England in 1066, so his company were Normans.

clue.text: " With too much knowledge for the side" (Pope)

definitions.text: " With too much knowledge for the side" (Pope)

parts.words: With too much knowledge for the side
parts.note: Pope's Essay on Man describes man as having too much knowledge to sit on the doubter's side; the dash marks the missing word

explanation.surface: A line of poetry by Alexander Pope with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue has a dash before 'side': the solver fills in the gap in Pope's line from Essay on Man.
explanation.definitionFit: In Pope's Essay on Man, man is 'With too much knowledge for the sceptic side', i.e. that of the doubter.

parts.note: the breathing tube from throat to lungs must be kept clear for one to stay alive

explanation.surface: A breathing route that must stay open to survive.
explanation.definitionFit: The trachea, or windpipe, carries air to the lungs, so it must stay clear for breathing to continue.

clue.text: Morton's choice at the parting of the ways

definitions.meaning: Archbishop Morton's tax argument left two options both leading to the same outcome
the point where a road splits into two branches

explanation.surface: Someone named Morton must choose where the road divides.
explanation.walkthrough: Morton's Fork is named for Henry VII's minister John Morton: the lavish could pay tax, and so could the thrifty, who must have savings.
explanation.definitionFit: A Morton's fork is a choice between two equally bad options, and a fork is also where a road divides.

parts.note: Prospero's speech in Shakespeare's Tempest says the world will melt away like this insubstantial pageant; the dash marks the missing word

explanation.surface: A quoted line from Shakespeare's The Tempest with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed clue ends the quotation with a dash: fill the gap from Prospero's 'Our revels now are ended' speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Prospero says the world shall dissolve 'and, like this insubstantial pageant faded, leave not a rack behind', meaning vanished.

parts.note: a trade union blacks goods or firms when it forbids its members to handle them
a guard is someone posted to keep watch

explanation.surface: A night watchman barred by his union suffers ill-treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: In British trade-union use, to black something is to boycott it.
explanation.definitionFit: To blackguard someone, an old verb, is to revile or insult them abusively.

definitions.meaning: the ready, or readies, is slang for money in hand
a ... deal is paid at once rather than on credit

explanation.surface: Something prepared so that a bill is paid at once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' looks like an adjective; it is British slang for money, as in 'the ready'.
explanation.definitionFit: 'The ready' is old slang for money, and a deal paid on the spot rather than on account is a cash one.

definitions.meaning: read as of the beast: the male of cattle is a familiar animal

explanation.surface: An exclamation at some horrible eye lotion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beastly' reads as horrid but here means 'a beast': the male bovine. Both readings are nouns in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A bull is a male bovine beast, and bull is also slang for nonsense, like eyewash.

clue.text: He's counted as a batman on paper

definitions.text: He's counted as a batman on paper

parts.words: He's counted as a batman on paper
parts.note: a nobleman of fiction, a Count who turns into a bat, existing only in a novel

explanation.surface: A soldier-servant is recorded in the books as on the roster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'counted' puns on the title Count, and 'batman' is not an officer's servant but a man who becomes a bat; 'on paper' means in Bram Stoker's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Bram Stoker's vampire Count turns into a bat, so he is a literary man-bat with a noble title.

parts.note: suggests a horse race lost narrowly, but means caned with a whistling stroke by a headmaster

explanation.surface: A racehorse narrowly outrun at the finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by a head' suggests a close race; here a head is a headmaster, and the beating is with a cane.
explanation.definitionFit: To swish is to flog with a cane or birch, the sound of the stroke giving the word.

parts.note: Dis is the Roman god of the underworld and a name for the underworld itself
plays are dramas

explanation.surface: Some theatre productions about the realm of the dead.
explanation.definitionFit: Exhibits or puts on view, the same as shows does as a verb.

clue.text: C.O.'s sister-in-law, Judy, versed in Kipling

definitions.text: C.O.'s sister-in-law, Judy, versed in Kipling

parts.words: C.O.'s sister-in-law, Judy, versed in Kipling
parts.note: Kipling's poem The Ladies says the Colonel's Lady and Judy are sisters under their skins; 'versed' means in verse

explanation.surface: A commanding officer's relative by marriage is well read in Kipling.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's 'The Ladies' ends 'For the Colonel's Lady an' Judy ___ Are sisters under their skins'; 'sister-in-law' is figurative, and 'versed' means 'in verse', not 'knowledgeable'.
explanation.definitionFit: Judy is the common soldier's girl in Kipling's 'The Ladies', named alongside the Colonel's Lady as a sister under the skin.
